newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Coffee price rise seen denting Russia bean imports.
newsitem.headline: Coffee price rise seen denting Russia bean imports.

text.p: Russia's coffee bean imports are likely to be hit if world prices remain high or increase further, a major coffee importer to Russia said on Wednesday.

Officials at Swiss-based Inter-Link, a trader specialising in imports of green coffee beans to Eastern Europe, said that Russian coffee roasters were more price-sensitive than roasters in the West, and would buy less if prices remained high.
"The coffee market at the moment is definitely putting a brake on demand (from Russian roasters)," Inter-Link president Hans De Heer said.
"Coffee beans have nearly doubled in price over the last few months, and we have seen some slowing in Russian purchases as a result," Yves Greppin, the group's managing partner added.

Second-month arabica coffee futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange rose to a peak of over 209 cents per pound in March, the highest since frosts ravaged crops in Brazil, the world's largest producer, in 1994.
The market began the year at around 134 cents/lb. On Wednesday second-month futures were only just off the year's highs at 203 cents/lb.

Russia is still a relatively small player on the coffee bean market, with the bulk of the country's coffee imports coming in pre-packaged, granulated form. Coffee also lags far behind tea in the hot drink market.
But the number of Russian roasting companies is on the rise and Inter-Link sees strong market potential in the coffee bean import business.
"We have seen a significant increase in roasted coffee consumption recently as opposed to instant coffee, which is a good sign for us and for roasters," Greppin said.
Official statistics showed Russia imported 25,000 tonnes of coffee beans from countries outside the Commonwealth of Independent States in 1996, down slightly from the 26,000 in 1995.
Heer said the market could grow strongly as roasting activity in Russia picked up, but added that a lot would depend on the price.
"If the world price of coffee comes down, then bean imports will grow. By how much depends on the price," he said.
Russian roasters are more price-sensitive than their western competitors because they are more reluctant to hand on raw material cost increases to customers, Greppin said.
"Most Russians just would not be able to afford it," he said.
Trading companies vying for a share of the Russian coffee bean market face the added challenge of having to compete with the government, Heer said.

He said Moscow was planning in 1997 to sell off state reserves of coffee beans which were over four years old, likely to involve several thousand tonnes. If trading firms charged too much, roasters would seek supplies from the reserves, he said.

"But if the international price of coffee comes down, we will have the opportunity to increase our market share, because there is likely to be a delay before reserve prices come down too," Heer said. --Mike Collett-White, Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520
